$$
\begin{aligned}s & =4{t}^{3/2} \\ {t}^{3/2} & =\frac{s}{4} \\ t & ={(\frac{s}{4})}^{2/3}.\end{aligned}
$$

 

The vector function that parametrizes $r(t)$ by its arc length is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}R(s) & =r({(\frac{s}{4})}^{2/3}) \\  & =[6{(\frac{s}{4})}^{2/3}-6]\,i+4{[{(\frac{s}{4})}^{2/3}-1]}^{3/2}\,j+2\,k \\  & =6[{(\frac{s}{4})}^{2/3}-1]\,i+4{[{(\frac{s}{4})}^{2/3}-1]}^{3/2}\,j+2\,k.\end{aligned}
$$

 

So, the $x$-component of $R$ is

$$
6[{(\frac{s}{4})}^{2/3}-1].
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-93649b9b-4496-5be5-8efe-dc54d74802dd"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id $t=\frac{\sqrt{2s}}{3}.$

The vector function that pametrizes the curve $r(t)$ by its arc length $s,$ with $s\ge 0,$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}R(s) & =r(\frac{\sqrt{2s}}{3}) \\  & =⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡(3\cdot \frac{\sqrt{2s}}{3})-3\cdot \frac{\sqrt{2s}}{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3\cdot \frac{\sqrt{2s}}{3}),\,\operatorname{cos}⁡(3\cdot \frac{\sqrt{2s}}{3})+3\cdot \frac{\sqrt{2s}}{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3\cdot \frac{\sqrt{2s}}{3})⟩ \\  & =⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{2s})-\sqrt{2s}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\sqrt{2s}),\,\operatorname{cos}⁡(\sqrt{2s})+\sqrt{2s}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{2s})⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

 

So, the $y$-component of $R$ is

$$
\operatorname{cos}⁡(\sqrt{2s})+\sqrt{2s}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{2s}).
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-b84fca7e-39f0-5846-a5a5-8d1c1f76b531"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id $s$ from $r(0)$ to $r(t)$ is given by $s=\frac{3{t}^{2}}{2},$ find the corresponding unit tangent $T(s),$ parametrized by $s.$" :question/worked-solution "First, since $s=\frac{3{t}^{2}}{2},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{3{t}^{2}}{2} & =s \\ {t}^{2} & =\frac{2s}{3} \\ t & =\sqrt{\frac{2s}{3}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the vector function $R(s)$ that parametrizes $r(t)$ by its arc length is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}R(s) & =r(\sqrt{\frac{2s}{3}}) \\  & =⟨{(\sqrt{\frac{2s}{3}})}^{2}+3,\,\frac{1}{2}{(\sqrt{\frac{2s}{3}})}^{2}\,,1-{(\sqrt{\frac{2s}{3}})}^{2}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{2s}{3}+3,\,\frac{s}{3},\,1-\frac{2s}{3}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

   

Now, since the curve is parameterized by its arc length $s$, the unit tangent can be found as

$$
T(s)=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}s}R(s).
$$

So, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}T(s) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}s}R(s) \\  & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}s}(\frac{2s}{3}+3),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}s}(\frac{s}{3}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}s}(1-\frac{2s}{3})⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{2}{3},\,\frac{1}{3},\,-\frac{2}{3}⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{3}⟨2,\,1,\,-2⟩.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-65648327-28cf-5416-8e2f-6a1fc5001bde"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "First, we find ${r}^{′}(t)$ and its magnitude $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(5\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t))i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t))\,j+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-3\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t))k \\  & =5\cdot 4\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)\,i-4\cdot 4\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)\,j+3\cdot 4\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)\,k \\  & =20\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)\,i-16\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)\,j+12\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)\,k \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(20\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t))}^{2}+{(16\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t))}^{2}+{(12\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t))}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{400{cos}^{2}⁡(4t)+256{sin}^{2}⁡(4t)+144{sin}^{2}⁡(4t)} \\  & =\sqrt{400[{cos}^{2}⁡(4t)+{sin}^{2}⁡(4t)]} \\  & =20\end{aligned}

Next, we calculate the arc length of the curve from $0$ to $t:$

$$
\begin{aligned}s & ={\int }_{0}^{t}‖{r}^{′}(u)‖\,\text{d}u \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{t}20\,\text{d}u \\  & =20u\,{|}_{0}^{t} \\  & =20t\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}s & =20t \\ t & =\frac{s}{20}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}R(s) & =r(\frac{s}{20}) \\  & =5\operatorname{sin}⁡(4\cdot \frac{s}{20})i+4\operatorname{cos}⁡(4\cdot \frac{s}{20})j-3\operatorname{cos}⁡(4\cdot \frac{s}{20})k \\  & =5\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{s}{5})i+4\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{s}{5})j-3\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{s}{5})k.\end{aligned}

by its arc length $s?$" :question/worked-solution "First, we find ${r}^{′}(t)$ and its magnitude $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{3/2}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{4}{3}{t}^{3/2}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1)⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{3}{2}{t}^{1/2},\,2{t}^{1/2},\,0⟩ \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(\frac{3}{2}{t}^{1/2})}^{2}+{(2{t}^{1/2})}^{2}+(0)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{9}{4}t+4t} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{25}{4}t} \\  & =\frac{5}{2}\sqrt{t}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the arc length of the curve from $0$ to $t:$

$$
\begin{aligned}s & ={\int }_{0}^{t}‖{r}^{′}(u)‖\,\text{d}u \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{t}\frac{5}{2}\sqrt{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{5}{2}{\int }_{0}^{t}\sqrt{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{5}{3}\sqrt{{u}^{3}}\,{|}_{0}^{t} \\  & =\frac{5}{3}\sqrt{{t}^{3}}\end{aligned}
$$

Since $s=\frac{5}{3}\sqrt{{t}^{3}},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{5}{3}\sqrt{{t}^{3}} & =s \\ \sqrt{{t}^{3}} & =\frac{3s}{5} \\ t & ={(\frac{3s}{5})}^{2/3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the vector function that parametrizes $r(t)$ by its arc length is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}R(s) & =r({(\frac{3s}{5})}^{2/3}) \\  & =⟨{({(\frac{3s}{5})}^{2/3})}^{3/2},\,\frac{4}{3}{({(\frac{3s}{5})}^{2/3})}^{3/2},\,1⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{3s}{5},\,\frac{4}{3}\cdot \frac{3s}{5},\,1⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{3s}{5},\,\frac{4s}{5},\,1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-369bbd24-91f1-5851-8599-621408e0023b"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-369bbd24-91f1-5851-8599-621408e0023b" :answer-field/id #uuid "369bbd24-91f1-5851-8599-621408e0023b" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-e10e8c34-d7a5-5c32-a5fb-5487a2156990" :answer-field/choices ["answer-e10e8c34-d7a5-5c32-a5fb-5487a2156990" "answer-caf2317e-01bb-53d6-bd84-e85f0344d156" "answer-88524411-7322-5c13-a0d6-4635b37af634" "answer-9cf6e55a-b413-5aa8-ab0c-0067c9c7f83b" "answer-c64215ca-c1b2-57b5-bdd6-c53bbb436663"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-e10e8c34-d7a5-5c32-a5fb-5487a2156990" :answer/id #uuid "e10e8c34-d7a5-5c32-a5fb-5487a2156990" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "R(s)=⟨\frac{3s}{5},\,\frac{4s}{5},\,1⟩" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-caf2317e-01bb-53d6-bd84-e85f0344d156" :answer/id #uuid "caf2317e-01bb-53d6-bd84-e85f0344d156" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "R(s)=⟨\frac{s}{3},\,\frac{2s}{3},\,1⟩" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-88524411-7322-5c13-a0d6-4635b37af634" :answer/id #uuid "88524411-7322-5c13-a0d6-4635b37af634" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "R(s)=⟨\frac{s}{5},\,\frac{4s}{5},\,1⟩" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-9cf6e55a-b413-5aa8-ab0c-0067c9c7f83b" :answer/id #uuid "9cf6e55a-b413-5aa8-ab0c-0067c9c7f83b" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "R(s)=⟨\frac{s}{\sqrt{5}},\,\frac{2s}{\sqrt{5}},\,1⟩" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-c64215ca-c1b2-57b5-bdd6-c53bbb436663" :answer/id #uuid "c64215ca-c1b2-57b5-bdd6-c53bbb436663" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "R(s)=⟨s,\,\frac{4s}{3},\,1⟩" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186121001 :tutorial/content "Consider the curve $C$ parametrized by the vector function 

$$
\mathbf r(t) = \langle 2\sin t, \: 2\cos t, \: \sqrt{5} t\rangle, \qquad t \ge 0.
$$

 

For any $t >0,$ the arc length $s$ of $C$ from $\mathbf r(0)$ to $\mathbf r(t)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}s & ={\int }_{0}^{t}‖{r}^{′}(u)‖\,du \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{t}‖⟨2\operatorname{cos}⁡u,\,-2\operatorname{sin}⁡u,\,\sqrt{5}⟩‖\,du \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{t}\sqrt{(2\operatorname{cos}⁡u)^{2}+(-2\operatorname{sin}⁡u)^{2}+(\sqrt{5})^{2}}\,du \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{t}\sqrt{4({cos}^{2}⁡u+{sin}^{2}⁡u)+5}\,du \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{t}\sqrt{9}\,du \\  & =3u{|}_{0}^{t} \\  & =3t.\end{aligned}
$$

So, $s= 3t,$ or equivalently $t = \dfrac{s}{3}.$ 

Now, we can define a new vector function $\mathbf{R}$ as

$$
\mathbf R(s)= \mathbf r\left(\dfrac{s}{3}\right) = \left\langle 2\sin \left(\dfrac{s}{3}\right), \: 2\cos \left(\dfrac{s}{3}\right), \: \sqrt{5} \left(\dfrac{s}{3}\right) \right\rangle .
$$

The function $\mathbf{R}(s)$ gives us the *same* curve $C,$ but this time it is parameterized by the arc length $s.$

In general, if $\mathbf r(t)$ for $t\in [a,b]$ is a continuously differentiable vector function such that $\mathbf r'(t )\neq \mathbf{0},$ then to parametrize it in terms of arc length we perform the following steps:

1\. Compute $s = \displaystyle s(t) = \int_a^t\|\mathbf r'(u)\| \, \mathrm{d}u$

2\. Write $s = s(t)$ in the form $t=t(s)$

3\. Substitute $t=t(s)$ back into $\mathbf r(t)$ to get $\mathbf R(s)=\mathbf r(t(s))$

**Note:** One advantage of parametrizing a curve by its arc length is that the tangent vector is always a unit vector:

$$
\left\|\dfrac{\textrm{d}\mathbf R}{\textrm{d} s}\right\| = 1

$$

$$

$$
T(s)=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}s}R(s).
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}T(s) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}s}R(s) \\  & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}s}(\frac{2s}{3}+3),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}s}(\frac{s}{3}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}s}(1-\frac{2s}{3})⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{2}{3},\,\frac{1}{3},\,-\frac{2}{3}⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{3}⟨2,\,1,\,-2⟩.\end{aligned}

"First, we find ${r}^{′}(t)$ and its magnitude $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(5\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t))i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t))\,j+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-3\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t))k \\  & =5\cdot 4\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)\,i-4\cdot 4\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)\,j+3\cdot 4\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)\,k \\  & =20\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)\,i-16\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)\,j+12\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)\,k \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(20\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t))}^{2}+{(16\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t))}^{2}+{(12\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t))}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{400{cos}^{2}⁡(4t)+256{sin}^{2}⁡(4t)+144{sin}^{2}⁡(4t)} \\  & =\sqrt{400[{cos}^{2}⁡(4t)+{sin}^{2}⁡(4t)]} \\  & =20\end{aligned}

Next, we calculate the arc length of the curve from $0$ to $t:$

$$
\begin{aligned}s & ={\int }_{0}^{t}‖{r}^{′}(u)‖\,\text{d}u \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{t}20\,\text{d}u \\  & =20u\,{|}_{0}^{t} \\  & =20t\end{aligned}
$$

  

Now, since $s=20t$, we have that

$$
\begin{aligned}s & =20t \\ t & =\frac{s}{20}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the vector function that parametrizes $r(t)$ by its arc length is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}R(s) & =r(\frac{s}{20}) \\  & =5\operatorname{sin}⁡(4\cdot \frac{s}{20})i+4\operatorname{cos}⁡(4\cdot \frac{s}{20})j-3\operatorname{cos}⁡(4\cdot \frac{s}{20})k \\  & =5\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{s}{5})i+4\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{s}{5})j-3\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{s}{5})k.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-dff45dea-1e54-5748-adfe-76155f49648f"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id by its arc length $s?$" :question/worked-solution "First, we find ${r}^{′}(t)$ and its magnitude $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{3/2}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{4}{3}{t}^{3/2}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1)⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{3}{2}{t}^{1/2},\,2{t}^{1/2},\,0⟩ \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(\frac{3}{2}{t}^{1/2})}^{2}+{(2{t}^{1/2})}^{2}+(0)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{9}{4}t+4t} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{25}{4}t} \\  & =\frac{5}{2}\sqrt{t}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the arc length of the curve from $0$ to $t:$

$$
\begin{aligned}s & ={\int }_{0}^{t}‖{r}^{′}(u)‖\,\text{d}u \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{t}\frac{5}{2}\sqrt{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{5}{2}{\int }_{0}^{t}\sqrt{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{5}{3}\sqrt{{u}^{3}}\,{|}_{0}^{t} \\  & =\frac{5}{3}\sqrt{{t}^{3}}\end{aligned}
$$

Since $s=\frac{5}{3}\sqrt{{t}^{3}},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{5}{3}\sqrt{{t}^{3}} & =s \\ \sqrt{{t}^{3}} & =\frac{3s}{5} \\ t & ={(\frac{3s}{5})}^{2/3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the vector function that parametrizes $r(t)$ by its arc length is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}R(s) & =r({(\frac{3s}{5})}^{2/3}) \\  & =⟨{({(\frac{3s}{5})}^{2/3})}^{3/2},\,\frac{4}{3}{({(\frac{3s}{5})}^{2/3})}^{3/2},\,1⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{3s}{5},\,\frac{4}{3}\cdot \frac{3s}{5},\,1⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{3s}{5},\,\frac{4s}{5},\,1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :question/answer-fields ["answer-field-369bbd24-91f1-5851-8599-621408e0023b"] :db/ensure [:question/validate]} {:db/id "answer-field-369bbd24-91f1-5851-8599-621408e0023b" :answer-field/id #uuid "369bbd24-91f1-5851-8599-621408e0023b" :answer-field/key "selection" :answer-field/type :answer-field.type/radio :answer-field/correct "answer-e10e8c34-d7a5-5c32-a5fb-5487a2156990" :answer-field/choices ["answer-e10e8c34-d7a5-5c32-a5fb-5487a2156990" "answer-caf2317e-01bb-53d6-bd84-e85f0344d156" "answer-88524411-7322-5c13-a0d6-4635b37af634" "answer-9cf6e55a-b413-5aa8-ab0c-0067c9c7f83b" "answer-c64215ca-c1b2-57b5-bdd6-c53bbb436663"] :db/ensure [:answer-field/validate]} {:db/id "answer-e10e8c34-d7a5-5c32-a5fb-5487a2156990" :answer/id #uuid "e10e8c34-d7a5-5c32-a5fb-5487a2156990" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "R(s)=⟨\frac{3s}{5},\,\frac{4s}{5},\,1⟩" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-caf2317e-01bb-53d6-bd84-e85f0344d156" :answer/id #uuid "caf2317e-01bb-53d6-bd84-e85f0344d156" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "R(s)=⟨\frac{s}{3},\,\frac{2s}{3},\,1⟩" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-88524411-7322-5c13-a0d6-4635b37af634" :answer/id #uuid "88524411-7322-5c13-a0d6-4635b37af634" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "R(s)=⟨\frac{s}{5},\,\frac{4s}{5},\,1⟩" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-9cf6e55a-b413-5aa8-ab0c-0067c9c7f83b" :answer/id #uuid "9cf6e55a-b413-5aa8-ab0c-0067c9c7f83b" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "R(s)=⟨\frac{s}{\sqrt{5}},\,\frac{2s}{\sqrt{5}},\,1⟩" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id "answer-c64215ca-c1b2-57b5-bdd6-c53bbb436663" :answer/id #uuid "c64215ca-c1b2-57b5-bdd6-c53bbb436663" :answer/type :answer.type/math :answer/value "R(s)=⟨s,\,\frac{4s}{3},\,1⟩" :db/ensure [:answer/validate]} {:db/id 17592186121001 :tutorial/content "Consider the curve $C$ parametrized by the vector function 

$$
\mathbf r(t) = \langle 2\sin t, \: 2\cos t, \: \sqrt{5} t\rangle, \qquad t \ge 0.
$$

 

For any $t >0,$ the arc length $s$ of $C$ from $\mathbf r(0)$ to $\mathbf r(t)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}s & ={\int }_{0}^{t}‖{r}^{′}(u)‖\,du \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{t}‖⟨2\operatorname{cos}⁡u,\,-2\operatorname{sin}⁡u,\,\sqrt{5}⟩‖\,du \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{t}\sqrt{(2\operatorname{cos}⁡u)^{2}+(-2\operatorname{sin}⁡u)^{2}+(\sqrt{5})^{2}}\,du \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{t}\sqrt{4({cos}^{2}⁡u+{sin}^{2}⁡u)+5}\,du \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{t}\sqrt{9}\,du \\  & =3u{|}_{0}^{t} \\  & =3t.\end{aligned}
$$

So, $s= 3t,$ or equivalently $t = \dfrac{s}{3}.$ 

Now, we can define a new vector function $\mathbf{R}$ as

$$
\mathbf R(s)= \mathbf r\left(\dfrac{s}{3}\right) = \left\langle 2\sin \left(\dfrac{s}{3}\right), \: 2\cos \left(\dfrac{s}{3}\right), \: \sqrt{5} \left(\dfrac{s}{3}\right) \right\rangle .
$$

The function $\mathbf{R}(s)$ gives us the *same* curve $C,$ but this time it is parameterized by the arc length $s.$

In general, if $\mathbf r(t)$ for $t\in [a,b]$ is a continuously differentiable vector function such that $\mathbf r'(t )\neq \mathbf{0},$ then to parametrize it in terms of arc length we perform the following steps:

1\. Compute $s = \displaystyle s(t) = \int_a^t\|\mathbf r'(u)\| \, \mathrm{d}u$

2\. Write $s = s(t)$ in the form $t=t(s)$

3\. Substitute $t=t(s)$ back into $\mathbf r(t)$ to get $\mathbf R(s)=\mathbf r(t(s))$

**Note:** One advantage of parametrizing a curve by its arc length is that the tangent vector is always a unit vector:

$$
\left\|\dfrac{\textrm{d}\mathbf R}{\textrm{d} s}\right\| = 1
$$" :db/ensure [:tutorial/validate]} {:db/id 17592186120037 :activity/expected-seconds 900.0 :db/ensure [:activity/validate]}] "assertions" [["question-d79c5095-b4c8-55c2-88ef-92a621d4625c" :question/id #uuid "d79c5095-b4c8-55c2-88ef-92a621d4625c"] ["question-d79c5095-b4c8-55c2-88ef-92a621d4625c" :question/math-academy-id "q-34887"] ["question-d79c5095-b4c8-55c2-88ef-92a621d4625c" :question/problem "Consider the curve  $r(t)=(6t-6)\,i+4(t-1)^{3/2}\,j+2\,k,$ $t\ge 0,$ for which the arc length from $r(0)$ to $r(t)$ is given by $s=4{t}^{3/2}.$ Given that $R(s)$ is the parameterization of the given curve by its arc length $s,$ what is the $x$-component of $R?$"] ["question-d79c5095-b4c8-55c2-88ef-92a621d4625c" :question/worked-solution "First, since  $s=4{t}^{3/2}$,  we have that

$$

:question/problem "Given the curve $r(t)=⟨{t}^{2}+3,\,\frac{1}{2}{t}^{2},\,1-{t}^{2}⟩,$ $t\ge 0,$ for which the arc length $s$ from $r(0)$ to $r(t)$ is given by $s=\frac{3{t}^{2}}{2},$ find the corresponding unit tangent $T(s),$ parametrized by $s.$"] ["question-7ba59ca0-21f4-55ed-9a11-93e0f28f7d7a" :question/worked-solution "First, since $s=\frac{3{t}^{2}}{2},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{3{t}^{2}}{2} & =s \\ {t}^{2} & =\frac{2s}{3} \\ t & =\sqrt{\frac{2s}{3}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the vector function $R(s)$ that parametrizes $r(t)$ by its arc length is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}R(s) & =r(\sqrt{\frac{2s}{3}}) \\  & =⟨{(\sqrt{\frac{2s}{3}})}^{2}+3,\,\frac{1}{2}{(\sqrt{\frac{2s}{3}})}^{2}\,,1-{(\sqrt{\frac{2s}{3}})}^{2}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{2s}{3}+3,\,\frac{s}{3},\,1-\frac{2s}{3}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

   

Now, since the curve is parameterized by its arc length $s$, the unit tangent can be found as

$$
T(s)=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}s}R(s).
$$

So, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}T(s) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}s}R(s) \\  & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}s}(\frac{2s}{3}+3),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}s}(\frac{s}{3}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}s}(1-\frac{2s}{3})⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{2}{3},\,\frac{1}{3},\,-\frac{2}{3}⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{3}⟨2,\,1,\,-2⟩.\end{aligned}
$$"] ["question-7ba59ca0-21f4-55ed-9a11-93e0f28f7d7a" :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/moderate] ["answer-field-65648327-28cf-5416-8e2f-6a1fc5001bde" :answer-field/id #uuid $$
\begin{aligned}s & ={\int }_{0}^{t}‖{r}^{′}(u)‖\,\text{d}u \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{t}\frac{5}{2}\sqrt{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{5}{2}{\int }_{0}^{t}\sqrt{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{5}{3}\sqrt{{u}^{3}}\,{|}_{0}^{t} \\  & =\frac{5}{3}\sqrt{{t}^{3}}\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{5}{3}\sqrt{{t}^{3}} & =s \\ \sqrt{{t}^{3}} & =\frac{3s}{5} \\ t & ={(\frac{3s}{5})}^{2/3}.\end{aligned}
$$

its arc length $s?$" :question/worked-solution "First, we find $\mathbf{r}'(t)$ and its magnitude $\|\mathbf{r}'(t)\|\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =2\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t\operatorname{cos}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,i+2\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t\operatorname{sin}⁡t+\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,j \\  & =2(\operatorname{cos}⁡t-t\operatorname{sin}⁡t-\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\,i+2(\operatorname{sin}⁡t+t\operatorname{cos}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,j \\  & =-2t\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+2t\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =|2t|\sqrt{(-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2}+{cos}^{2}⁡t} \\  & =2t\end{aligned}
$$

Note that in the last step, we removed the absolute value bars since $t>0.$ 

Next, we calculate the arc length of the curve from $0$ to $t\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}s & ={\int }_{0}^{t}‖{r}^{′}(u)‖\,\text{d}u \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{t}2u\,\text{d}u \\  & ={u}^{2}{|}_{0}^{t} \\  & ={t}^{2}-0 \\  & ={t}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $s=t^2,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{t}^{2} & =s \\ t & =\pm \sqrt{s} \\ t & =\sqrt{s},\end{aligned}
$$

taking the positive root because $t>0.$  

Finally, the vector function that parametrizes $\mathbf r(t)$ by its arc length is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}R(s) & =r(\sqrt{s}) \\  & =2(\sqrt{s}\operatorname{cos}⁡\sqrt{s}-\operatorname{sin}⁡\sqrt{s})\,i+2(\sqrt{s}\operatorname{sin}⁡\sqrt{s}+\operatorname{cos}⁡\sqrt{s})\,j.\end{aligned}

"First, we find ${r}^{′}(t)$ and its magnitude $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =⟨\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{4}),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{1}{2}{t}^{4}+2),\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3-{t}^{4})⟩ \\  & =⟨4{t}^{3},\,2{t}^{3},\,-4{t}^{3}⟩ \\  & =2{t}^{3}⟨2,\,1,\,-2⟩ \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =|2{t}^{3}|\sqrt{{(2)}^{2}+{(1)}^{2}+(-2)^{2}} \\  & =2{t}^{3}\sqrt{4+1+4} \\  & =6{t}^{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we calculate the arc length of the curve from $0$ to $t:$

$$
\begin{aligned}s & ={\int }_{0}^{t}‖{r}^{′}(u)‖\,\text{d}u \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{t}6{u}^{3}\,\text{d}u \\  & =6{\int }_{0}^{t}{u}^{3}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{3}{2}{u}^{4}\,{|}_{0}^{t} \\  & =\frac{3}{2}{t}^{4}\end{aligned}
$$

Since $s=\frac{3}{2}{t}^{4}$ and $t\ge 0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{3}{2}{t}^{4} & =s \\ {t}^{4} & =\frac{2s}{3} \\ t & =\sqrt[4]{\frac{2s}{3}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the vector function that parametrizes $r(t)$ by its arc length is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}R(s) & =r(\sqrt[4]{\frac{2s}{3}}) \\  & =⟨{(\sqrt[4]{\frac{2s}{3}})}^{4},\,\frac{1}{2}{(\sqrt[4]{\frac{2s}{3}})}^{4}+2,\,3-{(\sqrt[4]{\frac{2s}{3}})}^{4}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{2s}{3},\,\frac{s}{3}+2,\,3-\frac{2s}{3}⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{3}⟨2s,\,s+6,\,9-2s⟩.\end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned}s & ={\int }_{0}^{t}‖{r}^{′}(u)‖\,\text{d}u \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{t}\sqrt{\frac{3}{2}}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{3}{2}}\cdot u{|}_{0}^{t} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{3}{2}}\,t\end{aligned}

$$

$$

$$

$$

17592186120576 :step/content {:db/id 17592186121001 :tutorial/content "Consider the curve $C$ parametrized by the vector function 

$$
\mathbf r(t) = \langle 2\sin t, \: 2\cos t, \: \sqrt{5} t\rangle, \qquad t \ge 0.
$$

 

For any $t >0,$ the arc length $s$ of $C$ from $\mathbf r(0)$ to $\mathbf r(t)$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}s & ={\int }_{0}^{t}‖{r}^{'}(u)‖\,du \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{t}‖⟨2\operatorname{cos}u,\,-2\operatorname{sin}u,\,\sqrt{5}⟩‖\,du \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{t}\sqrt{(2\operatorname{cos}u)^{2}+(-2\operatorname{sin}u)^{2}+(\sqrt{5})^{2}}\,du \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{t}\sqrt{4({cos}^{2}u+{sin}^{2}u)+5}\,du \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{t}\sqrt{9}\,du \\  & =3u{|}_{0}^{t} \\  & =3t.\end{aligned}
$$

So, $s= 3t,$ or equivalently $t = \dfrac{s}{3}.$ 

Now, we can define a new vector function $\mathbf{R}$ as

$$

17592186045417] [17592186046659 1007 "Mathematical Methods for the Physical Sciences I" 17592186045417] [17592186046659 1008 "Mathematical Methods for the Physical Sciences I develops the core mathematical structures and analytical tools used throughout theoretical and applied physics. Building on calculus and introductory linear algebra, the course introduces vector geometry, multivariable analysis, and differential equations in a unified framework designed for modeling physical systems.
Students learn how mathematical concepts such as vector spaces, linear transformations, multivariable functions, and differential equations provide the language and computational techniques used to describe motion, fields, and dynamical processes. The course emphasizes connections between abstract mathematical ideas and the physical principles they support, preparing students for advanced study in classical mechanics, electromagnetism, and related areas of physics." 17592186045417] [17592186046659 1009 "The course begins with foundational topics that support later mathematical modeling in physics. Students study vector geometry in three-dimensional space, including equations of lines and planes and geometric relationships between them. These tools appear naturally in the description of trajectories, rays, and intersections of physical surfaces. Introductory set theory provides a precise language for describing mathematical structures and regions in space, supporting later work in multivariable analysis and probability.
Students then develop computational tools from linear algebra. Methods such as Gaussian elimination, matrix inverses, determinants, and LU factorization are used to analyze and solve systems of linear equations. These techniques arise when solving coupled equations in physical models, such as electrical circuits, mechanical systems with multiple interacting components, and discretized approximations of physical fields.
The course next develops the structure of vector spaces and linear transformations. Students study spans, bases, dimension, rank, and null spaces, and extend these ideas to abstract vector spaces. Linear maps and their matrix representations are examined, establishing the connection between geometric transformations and matrix algebra. These ideas culminate in the study of eigenvalues, eigenvectors, and matrix diagonalization, which are central tools for solving differential equations describing oscillations, normal modes of vibration, and stability of dynamical systems.
The course then turns to multivariable calculus and vector analysis. Students analyze functions of several variables, quadric surfaces, and coordinate transformations. Partial derivatives, gradients, and the multivariable chain rule are developed along with linear approximations and higher-order derivatives. These concepts describe how physical quantities such as temperature, pressure, or electric potential vary in space. Vector-valued functions and vector fields are studied together with curvature, divergence, and curl, providing the mathematical language used to describe velocity fields in fluid flow and electric and magnetic fields in electromagnetism.
Students then study multiple integration, focusing on double integrals and coordinate transformations such as polar coordinates. These techniques allow the computation of physical quantities distributed over regions, such as mass, charge, or probability density.
The final portion of the course introduces differential equations as models of dynamical systems. Students study first-order equations and qualitative behavior of solutions through phase-line analysis. Applications include motion under drag, gravitational attraction, electrical circuits, and population dynamics. The course concludes with second-order linear differential equations and oscillatory systems, including harmonic motion, damped oscillators, and resonance—fundamental mathematical models for vibrating strings, mechanical systems, and electromagnetic circuits." 17592186045417] [17592186046659 1012 154 17592186045417] [17592186046659 1013 "PS1" 17592186045417] [17592186046659 1014 #uuid
